full_text:
Interviewer:	I'll start off telling you a bit about what we're doing. We're interviewing women engineering students from all the disciplines. Are you – did you say you decided not to go on the placement?

Subject:	Yeah, I did.

Interviewer:	Well, the project focus is women going on the placement but we're interviewing people before they go and then when they're on placement – to find out their expectations and how that impacts on their career intentions and things like that. But we're also interviewing people about their experiences of higher education so far and why they decided to study engineering. So we want to interview some people not doing the placement too. I'll start off just asking you a few background questions really about why you wanted to do engineering then – is it commercial management you're doing?

Subject:	And quantity surveying, yeah.

Interviewer:	What A levels did you do?

Subject:	I did chemistry, biology and maths.

Interviewer:	OK, and what type of school did you go to?

Subject:	Erm, just a local comprehensive.

Interviewer:	Yeah, it wasn't a girls' school or anything like that?

Subject:	No.

Interviewer:	Ok, I think that you mentioned earlier that you have had some experience in the industry?

Subject:	Yeah, I worked last summer er for [company], down in London.

Interviewer:	OK I'll talk about that later. Are either of your parents engineers at all?

Subject:	No, they're both teachers.

Interviewer:	So when and why do you think that you decided to do engineering?

Subject:	Well, I didn't really –sort of after deciding which A levels – I didn't really know what I was going to do, sort of university wise. And my mum, she got a job with CITB, and so she kind of knew all about the construction industry and so she kind of thrust some leaflets under my nose and said what about this job? Er, I decided I wanted to come to [this university], and then I sort of found a course to match. So that's pretty the only reason I suppose.

Interviewer:	OK, what is it that appeals to you about construction then?

Subject:	Erm, well I've always sort of liked sort of buildings. Sort of – I want to go into the property market, eventually, when I'm older. And it's just kind of – I'm very much like – er I get on well with men, rather than girls and it's sort of a challenge being in a male dominated industry. Get a bit of a kick. Yeah, so…

Interviewer:	OK, did you ever consider doing any other types of engineering?

Subject:	Er no – well I did consider chemical engineering erm 'cos my brother did that at university – but I got fed up with sort of the sciences and it wasn't really as hands on as the construction industry.

Interviewer:	OK did you have any other influences, like careers advice – anything like that?

Subject:	No, not really.

Interviewer:	Did you know anything about engineering or would you have known anything about engineering if your brother hadn't been doing it and if your mother hadn't...?

Subject:	Oh no – yeah, I probably wouldn't have – I didn't even know what a QS was or – when my mum suggested it. So I didn't really know much – it sort of had to be researching when I decided which courses to do.

Interviewer:	OK, how did you – why did you decide to come to [this university]?

Subject:	Erm, I don't know it's just – it's quite a nice sort of a campus and erm I came round on an Open Day and it just had a really nice atmosphere around it and I fitted in, whereas at some of the other universities it didn't really feel like I could be there, and sort of call it home.

Interviewer:	When you first started doing engineering did you realise it was going to be so male dominated?

Subject:	Yeah, I got told, 'cos on the open day I was the only girl there and I got told that there was sort of 35 places but there was only – at that point, there was only 1 other girl doing the course. So I knew there was at least going to be 2 of us. So I did know it was going to be all guys but I got – well, I get on well with them. It doesn't seem to be a problem.

Interviewer:	OK. Do you think that more women should be encouraged to do engineering?

Subject:	Er yeah I think so but there's just not – there's not information around about it. Erm, 'cos I know – 'cos I know with my mum in CITB, she was – she was going round all the sort of local schools trying to drum up enthusiasm for it, and she sort of – she targeted the girls as well and it's sort of an extra check list.

Interviewer:	How do you think that more women can be encouraged then? Do you think it's by education?

Subject:	Yes, it's all the awareness about it. I don't – 'cos I know definitely in the construction industry – many people don't know kind of the different jobs involved. You know, it's just the way it is with it.

Interviewer:	OK, What characteristics do you think make a good engineer?

Subject:	Erm, I think you've got to be quite kind of strong minded and you've also got to be able to take things on the chin as well. Specially with all the banter the lads give you. It 's just kind of laid back and able to sort of think on your feet as well.

Interviewer:	Do you think that any of those characteristics are more male or female?

Subject:	Yeah, probably most of them are. I'm quite – I'm a laddish girl. So I don't – yeah, I don't think – if you're a bit kind of wet, you know, I don't think a girl would go far.

Interviewer:	OK, What do you think are the advantages or disadvantages of being a woman engineer?

Subject:	Erm, I dunno. Er, disadvantage – you do get like – there's a bit of a stereotype about women in the industry and its kind of you always get labelled. The one thing I've found is that I got – when I was getting sponsored, I got lots of info, I got lots of companies saying yeah we'll sponsor you – only because I was a girl. I know it's kind of – you know – oh that's looks better on our statistics. I don't – I didn't feel like they wanted me because of what I could do, it was just because I was a girl

Interviewer:	Yes. Did you find that quite patronising?

Subject:	Yeah, it was a bit. And some of the sort of older generation, in the industry, are very kind of er sexist. And – but they don't like – they don't do it on purpose but it's kind of because they're so used to just having just males, they'll always kind of refer to him or you know – and forget that there are actually girls there. That's one of the disadvantages. But I don't know – kind of the advantages are just – I get on well, like I say, with lads I think if there were too many women around me I don't think I could handle it. Especially if they get all bitchy.

Interviewer:	OK, has the course been what you expected it to be?

Subject:	Erm, probably more – I'm kind of – I was aware that it was very – there was a bit of business studies and economics mixed into that, which is one of the reasons I chose to do the CM course but yeah, I'm really enjoying it and I definitely, even though I'm not gonna stay QS'ing for sort of long after, it's not like my final career. Er, I'm glad I did the course, 'cos it's not – I've learnt so much more, other than just kind of construction, which is good.

Interviewer:	OK. What do you think has been the best and the worst things about the course?

Subject:	Erm, the work is pretty tough, because I've got about 19 hours a week and the coursework's a bit of nightmare, but the work's good and the lecturers – some of them, especially if you get sort of from other departments, like sort of the law and economics, er they're like – they weren't particularly good but the lecturers are really good from our department. They're really enthusiastic about it and enjoy teaching it which is good. So it makes me want to learn more.

Interviewer:	OK, have you been taught by any female lecturers?

Subject:	Yeah. Yeah, er [name]? Oh, sorry I can't think of her surname – she was a bit – she's a bit wet. So I really didn't get on very well with her because this is kind of – I can't see her in the industry, at all, and she was so kind of pathetic.

Interviewer:	Was she teaching a construction module?

Subject:	Yeah – yeah we were doing sort of measurement and she – she wouldn't be able to get order in the lecture theatre at all.

Interviewer:	So she wasn't a good role model?

Subject:	No, not at all. You know, she's nice enough but she didn't kind of have the spark that – to do well in the industry, for me.

Interviewer:	Do you think it'd be encouraging to have more female lecturers?

Subject:	Erm, yeah I suppose so.

Interviewer:	If they're good.

Subject:	Yeah, exactly because we don't have any – I don't think it really matters what sex they are, as long as they enjoy teaching and put that across, and the modules are good, it doesn't really matter which sort of gender they are at all.

Interviewer:	OK, do you think that the female lecturer treated you the same as the male lecturers?

Subject:	Er, yeah, I think so. I don't think there was any sort of discrimination about it.

Interviewer:	Do you think that the male lecturers have treated the male and female students the same?

Subject:	Erm, I think so. Some of the lads would disagree with me and it's sort of course work grades and they were like it's only 'cos you're a girl. But I don't think so, it's just – it doesn't really matter which…

Interviewer:	OK. Have you got a personal tutor?

Subject:	Yeah, it's a man.

Interviewer:	Would you rather have a female personal tutor?

Subject:	No, I'm not really bothered. Erm, my tutor's a nightmare – I don't like him. He doesn't really kind of get enthusiastic about it. So…

Interviewer:	OK, do you go to anyone else, if you need it, for advice and things?

Subject:	Yeah, I tend to go to the warden of, [name] because he's a junior and he's one of my lecturers as well, so I tend to go to him because I was in the (?) last year. So I go and do that as well – any sort of work related I go to him…

Interviewer:	OK, is there anything or anyone that you would say has been like the biggest influence on you since you started the degree?

Subject:	Er, not really. I suppose the only thing is [lecturer] did a law module, last semester, and that kind of – well I'm quite interested in the legal side of it – so he's kind of influenced me in that.

Interviewer:	OK have you had to do a lot of group work?

Subject:	Yeah. Loads. Yeah, usually I'm the only girl in the group so…

Interviewer:	Yeah, do you get put into groups or do you choose people?

Subject:	It's kind of 50/50 most of the time. Erm, if I do choose it's usually - my house mate's on my course. So there'll be him and a few other lads and me.

Interviewer:	Do you consciously decide not to work with the women? Did you say how many women are on your course?

Subject:	Yeah there's 2 others. Erm, I have got groups that they got – that they're in. I get on well with them. It's just – it's more kind of convenience, people sort of living round me that I choose. It's just easier than travelling and stuff – organising to meet.

Interviewer:	Do you think that men and women bring different characteristics to group work?

Subject:	Yeah, definitely. Erm, whereas I think the other girls, definitely in the group, have sort of – they want to finish everything off and make it look neater – I don't. I'm not that way – you know, I just do my bit and leave it for someone else to faff around with. But yeah, definitely. I think I'm a lot more logical than some of the guys – setting out work and things.

Interviewer:	OK, have you had any particularly good or bad experiences of group work?

Subject:	Erm, no they've all just sort of been – you get the work done and that's it. Erm, it's annoying when you get sort of a couple of people that just don't do anything and don't want to get involved. There's one guy and he just doesn't do anything, and he (lost words), which was a bit annoying.

Interviewer:	What do you think are the advantages or the disadvantages of doing group work?

Subject:	Erm, you've definitely got to be able to have like people skills erm when you're working. So group work – you're practising that all the time and learning to kind of organise yourself. Cos it is like – that's one thing I've learnt from group work, you have to organise yourself much more than if you were doing it on your own. You've got to arrange meetings and work out who's doing what. So it's definitely – you've got to be able to do that in the industry – yeah, but the disadvantages of that is that if you can't make a meeting or you know, you have to faff around with everything. It's much simpler just to kind of do a bit here and there, when you're on your own, you can't do that with the group work.

Interviewer:	OK, how did you decide not to go on a placement?

Subject:	Well, the company I was working with over the summer, I didn't really get on – they were really large company and I was like down in London, on one of their biggest jobs. And it just kind of – I felt like – it wasn't the sort of company that I wanted to work for and I don't – I think if I went on a placement with them. I think if I went on a placement with them, I'd probably wouldn't – I'd jack the whole thing in. 'Cos it was just too big for me. I prefer the sort of smaller contractors, because I've got a job erm with a local one, from my home town, for over the summer and possibly when I graduate – plus I want to get my degree out the way (yeah). It's sort of another thing at [this university], that I just want to get out working properly and not have to have a year out and come back do your – you know, finish off your degree. It's a bit of – it's a bit of too big an interruption for me. I'd sort of lose all my motivation to work.

Interviewer:	Did you say you were a sponsored student?

Subject:	Yeah, I was, yeah, but I've stopped that now. Well I've gone onto the 3 – the 3 year course.

Interviewer:	Was that to do with the placement?

Subject:	Yeah. If I wasn't on the placement, then they didn't want to sponsor me. Which is fair enough – they don't want to give me money if I'm not gonna work for them.

Interviewer:	Were they quite reasonable with you about that then?

Subject:	Yeah, it was – it was quite a joint decision between er the kind of advisor that I had that it sort of – I hadn't – I'd enjoyed working but I didn't kind of enjoy the environment that the company had. And I know, from other students who are sponsored with them, they don't like working for them either, but they want to do their placements, so I think it was sort of 50/50, I suppose.

Interviewer:	What was it, do you think, about their environment that you didn't get on with?

Subject:	I don't know. I think it was just cos it was so large, and the company's very much kind of – they don't really care about their employees very much. They've got quite a big turnover – I don't want to slag them off but yeah, the people that I was working with, most of them were saying, probably in 6 months time they wouldn't be working for them. And it wasn't – it wasn't a very – it wasn't positive at all. And there was 2 – there was 2 kinds of departments in the offices that I was working with and they didn't get on. There was always rivalry and I was kind of – I was working for both of them to get a bit more experience and kind of everyone was slagging off everyone else. I wasn't – I don't – I wouldn't be able to last a year working for them if it carried on like that.

Interviewer:	What were the gender proportions like?

Subject:	Er, they were mostly men like all their kind of – the QS's and the engineers were all men. There were a few secretaries. They were a bit bitchy but there was one commercial manager, and she was a woman, and she was sort of – and she was very aware of the fact that er she's had to work hard to get where she is and she had a bit of a chip on her shoulder about that really, yeah. Yeah, she was alright but I – you know I got on better with the males, rather than the females.

Interviewer:	OK, what would you say were the best things and the worst things about doing that placement?

Subject:	Erm, the best thing would be the experience. It was my kind of first proper, on-site QS'ing that I'd done and I got – I kind of delved into other areas, sort of health & safety, which you don't really tend to learn when you're at university. And it's amazing how kind of – I didn't think I learnt very much in my first year and I thought the modules were really kind of airy fairy but it's actually amazing how much I put into practice when I was working and how kind of everything seemed to make a bit more sense. Which is good. But I think just kind of well summer work – because it was down in London as well, so commuting was kind of a nightmare as well – sort of the early mornings – it didn't really agree with my system.

Interviewer:	Have you used anything that you've learnt from the placement, when you've come back to Uni?

Subject:	Yeah, definitely. I've kind of – all my measurement skills are kind of much more – I can do it a lot quicker than what I used to be able to. Yeah, and kind of all the sort of practicalness and stuff, like materials and stuff that you learn when you're on site, you can come back and you know, you know what people are going on about now, which is good.

Interviewer:	OK – the experience didn't put you off?

Subject:	No not at all. It's just kind of – I definitely – I don't think I can see myself staying as a QS kind of through my whole career and it's – it's a good job there's times like you kind of float in and out of it, particularly if you get chartership at the end of it. You know, I can do kind of more erm kind of the private sector and kind of float from contract to contract and you go travelling as well. So much site (?) but then sort of in about 10 years – 5/10 years after I'll try and get into the property market.

Interviewer:	OK, do you think that the way that you're taught and the whole sort of educational experience, reflects what it's like in industry?

Subject:	No, not at all. It's – it's – so kind of, everything that you learn – kind of all the theory and stuff it's actually – it's not done like that on like – in the sort of industry. They cut corners a lot and you know, with it being sort of (?) I had to do all this measurement – half the stuff I don't think you use when you're actually in the industry – it seems really pointless to learn about it.

Interviewer:	Do you think it should be more geared to prepare you for the industry?

Subject:	Yeah, I think so – I – you know, they're doing a good job at the moment because it's cut and run by sort of totally different construction companies, they do have a say sort of what modules that they think, you know, that they want teaching – which is good. Which sort of most other courses don't have. But yeah, they sort of stand there and it's you know, it's sort of – I don't know, it needs a tweak a bit.

Interviewer:	OK, I think you've said a bit about what type of company you'd like to work for when you finish your course, but what sort of characteristics or things will you particularly be looking for?

Subject:	Er, well just kind of a bit more kind of insular in a way – it's like that's all the small companies that you know, have got better kind of sort of customer relations – sort of people skills with their workers. I don't think it's – you can't really, in a bigger company it's much more erm difficult to sort of get up the hierarchy whereas with a smaller one you can kind of go and you can, you know, you can become the top QS a lot quicker than in a bigger company. I think once you've reached that, then you can go back into the big company and you 're actually valued a bit more – yeah.

Interviewer:	So it's probably easier to make a name for yourself?

Subject:	Yeah, definitely.

Interviewer:	OK, what aspects of the teaching and advice that you've had, do you think will help you when you go into the industry?

Subject:	Oh, I dunno. It's just – I think we definitely learn a lot about sort of people skills and we've got a team building erm trip in the Lake District, next week. I think I'm dreading it (are you?). You know it's like some sort of team building exercises and things its very much sort of business studies minded – especially this semester, which is good. So I'm learning a bit more of kind of – sort of behind the scenes a bit – how the construction industry works, which is good. I enjoy that bit.

Interviewer:	OK, in terms of your career then what do you see yourself doing in 5 years time?

Subject:	Well, after erm Uni I'm gonna kind of go – hopefully I can get a job with my local contractor at my own town. Work for them for a few years, go travelling hopefully and then, probably, I want to – by the time I'm 30 I want to be in the property market and sort of redeveloping houses. Because I feel I've been – you know, I've got all this knowledge about the construction industry – I can use it to my advantage, you know and I have contacts in the industry, which always help.

Interviewer:	Yeah, is that sort of your ideal career then?

Subject:	Yeah, definitely.

Interviewer:	Do you think that there will be any barriers preventing you achieving that?

Subject:	Er, at the moment it's financial – you've got to have the capital to invest in the first place. Erm, but I'm quite lucky I've inherited enough so I can, you know, at least get one step on the ladder, so that's good.

Interviewer:	Excellent. Would you like to work abroad or do you just want to go…?

Subject:	Well - yeah, I wouldn't mind especially like somewhere like where it's hot. But that's the beauty of QS'ing as well. Because it's – you know – everything is a standard way of doing it you can work in other countries quite easily. Yeah, I would – you know, if there was a job going I definitely would.

Interviewer:	Do you think that the career prospects are good in what you want to go into?

Subject:	Yeah, I think so. You know there's always kind of jobs going – there's plenty in the papers and things. Cos there's so many companies as well and I think – I think the turnover is quite sort of rapid, so there are always jobs available.

Interviewer:	OK, what about the prospects once you're into the industry then?

Subject:	Yeah I think it's good. I mean you do kind of – they encourage you to get your sort of chartership and they encourage you to go on courses. You get little ticks in your boxes for things, which is good. And CITB kind of help with all that as well. And you can do health and safety training and definitely, you can climb the ladder if you want to.

Interviewer:	OK, are you happy with all the career choices you've made so far? Would you do anything differently if you had to do it all again?

Subject:	Yeah, I probably wouldn't have chosen the company that I was sponsored by if I knew a bit more about it. 'Cos that's – you know I feel they didn't want me for who I was and I felt like, you know I was getting treated like that when I was working there. Erm, I think I would have chosen a smaller company. Yeah, definitely.

Interviewer:	Do you think that the reason you were treated like that had anything to do with being female or do you just think it was just because you were a student or just the company?

Subject:	I think – there was that factor, you know, they only employed me because I was a girl and it – you know it looked good on their statistics, because I know, from my mum, they do get kind of extra bonuses for having female employees and they have an incentive. I definitely think it was – especially some of the older staff were like that.

Interviewer:	What 5 words would you use to describe the construction industry?

Subject:	Oh God. Erm, I suppose hard work is one (Yeah). Erm, I don't know, I suppose quite domineering and well it's fun as well and it's manual – hands on. That's 5 or 4?

Interviewer:	When you say domineering, what do you mean by that?

Subject:	Well, you have to be quite kind of forceful a bit, especially working with the men you've got to be quite quick witted and you know, show that you've got a bit of power – and it's quite a power trip when you're working, especially when you're working with the labourers - you know, they've come in and asked me for money. And you can say, well no, and you've got to be able to put your foot down but you've also got to be able to kind of take everything on the chin. You're always gonna get banter.

Interviewer:	Do you think there is conflict between being a good professional in the industry and being feminine?

Subject:	Yeah, I felt, when I was working that they didn't – er it was weird because I felt like they only employed me because I was a girl and yet they didn't want me to act feminine. And so I kind of – you know – when I was going – you know getting – going out for drinks and stuff it was always – everyone kind of frowned upon iy and there was – you know – I was trying to be like one of the lads, you know, but there is this type of – they took it as you know, I was going on all these dates and things and you know - it was – they just didn't want me to act feminine. Kind of – you know – I got, when I was working there I got sort of advised how to dress – it was just like you know, well surely I can just sort of – if I want to wear a skirt, I can. You know there's definitely that aspect to it, yeah.

Interviewer:	OK, do you think that the engineering culture is masculine?

Subject:	Yeah, definitely. I mean only due to the fact that sort of the actual work involves kind of – well hands on skills and things. So it's - I don't think it's because there's all these males in the industry it's just that's sort of the nature of the job.

Interviewer:	Do you think then that it will stay like that?

Subject:	I think so yeah, I know the year below, there's a few more girls on the course, which is good, but I think it's mainly gonna be sort of male dominated. I don't think it's gonna change,

Interviewer:	OK, that's everything I need – thank you very much.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er yeah I think so but there's just not – there's not information around about it. Erm, 'cos I know – 'cos I know with my mum in CITB, she was – she was going round all the sort of local schools trying to drum up enthusiasm for it, and she sort of – she targeted the girls as well and it's sort of an extra check list.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: How do you think that more women can be encouraged then? Do you think it's by education?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes, it's all the awareness about it. I don't – 'cos I know definitely in the construction industry – many people don't know kind of the different jobs involved. You know, it's just the way it is with it.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, What characteristics do you think make a good engineer?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, I think you've got to be quite kind of strong minded and you've also got to be able to take things on the chin as well. Specially with all the banter the lads give you. It 's just kind of laid back and able to sort of think on your feet as well.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that any of those characteristics are more male or female?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, probably most of them are. I'm quite – I'm a laddish girl. So I don't – yeah, I don't think – if you're a bit kind of wet, you know, I don't think a girl would go far.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, What do you think are the advantages or disadvantages of being a woman engineer?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, I dunno. Er, disadvantage – you do get like – there's a bit of a stereotype about women in the industry and its kind of you always get labelled. The one thing I've found is that I got – when I was getting sponsored, I got lots of info, I got lots of companies saying yeah we'll sponsor you – only because I was a girl. I know it's kind of – you know – oh that's looks better on our statistics. I don't – I didn't feel like they wanted me because of what I could do, it was just because I was a girl

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yes. Did you find that quite patronising?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, it was a bit. And some of the sort of older generation, in the industry, are very kind of er sexist. And – but they don't like – they don't do it on purpose but it's kind of because they're so used to just having just males, they'll always kind of refer to him or you know – and forget that there are actually girls there. That's one of the disadvantages. But I don't know – kind of the advantages are just – I get on well, like I say, with lads I think if there were too many women around me I don't think I could handle it. Especially if they get all bitchy.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, has the course been what you expected it to be?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, probably more – I'm kind of – I was aware that it was very – there was a bit of business studies and economics mixed into that, which is one of the reasons I chose to do the CM course but yeah, I'm really enjoying it and I definitely, even though I'm not gonna stay QS'ing for sort of long after, it's not like my final career. Er, I'm glad I did the course, 'cos it's not – I've learnt so much more, other than just kind of construction, which is good.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK. What do you think has been the best and the worst things about the course?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, the work is pretty tough, because I've got about 19 hours a week and the coursework's a bit of nightmare, but the work's good and the lecturers – some of them, especially if you get sort of from other departments, like sort of the law and economics, er they're like – they weren't particularly good but the lecturers are really good from our department. They're really enthusiastic about it and enjoy teaching it which is good. So it makes me want to learn more.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, have you been taught by any female lecturers?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah. Yeah, er [name]? Oh, sorry I can't think of her surname – she was a bit – she's a bit wet. So I really didn't get on very well with her because this is kind of – I can't see her in the industry, at all, and she was so kind of pathetic.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Was she teaching a construction module?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah – yeah we were doing sort of measurement and she – she wouldn't be able to get order in the lecture theatre at all.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: So she wasn't a good role model?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No, not at all. You know, she's nice enough but she didn't kind of have the spark that – to do well in the industry, for me.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think it'd be encouraging to have more female lecturers?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, yeah I suppose so.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: If they're good.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, exactly because we don't have any – I don't think it really matters what sex they are, as long as they enjoy teaching and put that across, and the modules are good, it doesn't really matter which sort of gender they are at all.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, do you think that the female lecturer treated you the same as the male lecturers?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er, yeah, I think so. I don't think there was any sort of discrimination about it.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that the male lecturers have treated the male and female students the same?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, I think so. Some of the lads would disagree with me and it's sort of course work grades and they were like it's only 'cos you're a girl. But I don't think so, it's just – it doesn't really matter which…

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK. Have you got a personal tutor?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, it's a man.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Would you rather have a female personal tutor?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No, I'm not really bothered. Erm, my tutor's a nightmare – I don't like him. He doesn't really kind of get enthusiastic about it. So…

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, do you go to anyone else, if you need it, for advice and things?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, I tend to go to the warden of, [name] because he's a junior and he's one of my lecturers as well, so I tend to go to him because I was in the (?) last year. So I go and do that as well – any sort of work related I go to him…

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, is there anything or anyone that you would say has been like the biggest influence on you since you started the degree?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er, not really. I suppose the only thing is [lecturer] did a law module, last semester, and that kind of – well I'm quite interested in the legal side of it – so he's kind of influenced me in that.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK have you had to do a lot of group work?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah. Loads. Yeah, usually I'm the only girl in the group so…

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah, do you get put into groups or do you choose people?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: It's kind of 50/50 most of the time. Erm, if I do choose it's usually - my house mate's on my course. So there'll be him and a few other lads and me.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you consciously decide not to work with the women? Did you say how many women are on your course?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah there's 2 others. Erm, I have got groups that they got – that they're in. I get on well with them. It's just – it's more kind of convenience, people sort of living round me that I choose. It's just easier than travelling and stuff – organising to meet.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that men and women bring different characteristics to group work?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, definitely. Erm, whereas I think the other girls, definitely in the group, have sort of – they want to finish everything off and make it look neater – I don't. I'm not that way – you know, I just do my bit and leave it for someone else to faff around with. But yeah, definitely. I think I'm a lot more logical than some of the guys – setting out work and things.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, have you had any particularly good or bad experiences of group work?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, no they've all just sort of been – you get the work done and that's it. Erm, it's annoying when you get sort of a couple of people that just don't do anything and don't want to get involved. There's one guy and he just doesn't do anything, and he (lost words), which was a bit annoying.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What do you think are the advantages or the disadvantages of doing group work?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, you've definitely got to be able to have like people skills erm when you're working. So group work – you're practising that all the time and learning to kind of organise yourself. Cos it is like – that's one thing I've learnt from group work, you have to organise yourself much more than if you were doing it on your own. You've got to arrange meetings and work out who's doing what. So it's definitely – you've got to be able to do that in the industry – yeah, but the disadvantages of that is that if you can't make a meeting or you know, you have to faff around with everything. It's much simpler just to kind of do a bit here and there, when you're on your own, you can't do that with the group work.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, how did you decide not to go on a placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Well, the company I was working with over the summer, I didn't really get on – they were really large company and I was like down in London, on one of their biggest jobs. And it just kind of – I felt like – it wasn't the sort of company that I wanted to work for and I don't – I think if I went on a placement with them. I think if I went on a placement with them, I'd probably wouldn't – I'd jack the whole thing in. 'Cos it was just too big for me. I prefer the sort of smaller contractors, because I've got a job erm with a local one, from my home town, for over the summer and possibly when I graduate – plus I want to get my degree out the way (yeah). It's sort of another thing at [this university], that I just want to get out working properly and not have to have a year out and come back do your – you know, finish off your degree. It's a bit of – it's a bit of too big an interruption for me. I'd sort of lose all my motivation to work.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Did you say you were a sponsored student?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, I was, yeah, but I've stopped that now. Well I've gone onto the 3 – the 3 year course.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Was that to do with the placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah. If I wasn't on the placement, then they didn't want to sponsor me. Which is fair enough – they don't want to give me money if I'm not gonna work for them.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Were they quite reasonable with you about that then?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, it was – it was quite a joint decision between er the kind of advisor that I had that it sort of – I hadn't – I'd enjoyed working but I didn't kind of enjoy the environment that the company had. And I know, from other students who are sponsored with them, they don't like working for them either, but they want to do their placements, so I think it was sort of 50/50, I suppose.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What was it, do you think, about their environment that you didn't get on with?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I don't know. I think it was just cos it was so large, and the company's very much kind of – they don't really care about their employees very much. They've got quite a big turnover – I don't want to slag them off but yeah, the people that I was working with, most of them were saying, probably in 6 months time they wouldn't be working for them. And it wasn't – it wasn't a very – it wasn't positive at all. And there was 2 – there was 2 kinds of departments in the offices that I was working with and they didn't get on. There was always rivalry and I was kind of – I was working for both of them to get a bit more experience and kind of everyone was slagging off everyone else. I wasn't – I don't – I wouldn't be able to last a year working for them if it carried on like that.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What were the gender proportions like?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er, they were mostly men like all their kind of – the QS's and the engineers were all men. There were a few secretaries. They were a bit bitchy but there was one commercial manager, and she was a woman, and she was sort of – and she was very aware of the fact that er she's had to work hard to get where she is and she had a bit of a chip on her shoulder about that really, yeah. Yeah, she was alright but I – you know I got on better with the males, rather than the females.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, what would you say were the best things and the worst things about doing that placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, the best thing would be the experience. It was my kind of first proper, on-site QS'ing that I'd done and I got – I kind of delved into other areas, sort of health & safety, which you don't really tend to learn when you're at university. And it's amazing how kind of – I didn't think I learnt very much in my first year and I thought the modules were really kind of airy fairy but it's actually amazing how much I put into practice when I was working and how kind of everything seemed to make a bit more sense. Which is good. But I think just kind of well summer work – because it was down in London as well, so commuting was kind of a nightmare as well – sort of the early mornings – it didn't really agree with my system.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Have you used anything that you've learnt from the placement, when you've come back to Uni?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, definitely. I've kind of – all my measurement skills are kind of much more – I can do it a lot quicker than what I used to be able to. Yeah, and kind of all the sort of practicalness and stuff, like materials and stuff that you learn when you're on site, you can come back and you know, you know what people are going on about now, which is good.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK – the experience didn't put you off?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No not at all. It's just kind of – I definitely – I don't think I can see myself staying as a QS kind of through my whole career and it's – it's a good job there's times like you kind of float in and out of it, particularly if you get chartership at the end of it. You know, I can do kind of more erm kind of the private sector and kind of float from contract to contract and you go travelling as well. So much site (?) but then sort of in about 10 years – 5/10 years after I'll try and get into the property market.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, do you think that the way that you're taught and the whole sort of educational experience, reflects what it's like in industry?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No, not at all. It's – it's – so kind of, everything that you learn – kind of all the theory and stuff it's actually – it's not done like that on like – in the sort of industry. They cut corners a lot and you know, with it being sort of (?) I had to do all this measurement – half the stuff I don't think you use when you're actually in the industry – it seems really pointless to learn about it.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think it should be more geared to prepare you for the industry?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, I think so – I – you know, they're doing a good job at the moment because it's cut and run by sort of totally different construction companies, they do have a say sort of what modules that they think, you know, that they want teaching – which is good. Which sort of most other courses don't have. But yeah, they sort of stand there and it's you know, it's sort of – I don't know, it needs a tweak a bit.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, I think you've said a bit about what type of company you'd like to work for when you finish your course, but what sort of characteristics or things will you particularly be looking for?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er, well just kind of a bit more kind of insular in a way – it's like that's all the small companies that you know, have got better kind of sort of customer relations – sort of people skills with their workers. I don't think it's – you can't really, in a bigger company it's much more erm difficult to sort of get up the hierarchy whereas with a smaller one you can kind of go and you can, you know, you can become the top QS a lot quicker than in a bigger company. I think once you've reached that, then you can go back into the big company and you 're actually valued a bit more – yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: So it's probably easier to make a name for yourself?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, definitely.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, what aspects of the teaching and advice that you've had, do you think will help you when you go into the industry?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Oh, I dunno. It's just – I think we definitely learn a lot about sort of people skills and we've got a team building erm trip in the Lake District, next week. I think I'm dreading it (are you?). You know it's like some sort of team building exercises and things its very much sort of business studies minded – especially this semester, which is good. So I'm learning a bit more of kind of – sort of behind the scenes a bit – how the construction industry works, which is good. I enjoy that bit.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, in terms of your career then what do you see yourself doing in 5 years time?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Well, after erm Uni I'm gonna kind of go – hopefully I can get a job with my local contractor at my own town. Work for them for a few years, go travelling hopefully and then, probably, I want to – by the time I'm 30 I want to be in the property market and sort of redeveloping houses. Because I feel I've been – you know, I've got all this knowledge about the construction industry – I can use it to my advantage, you know and I have contacts in the industry, which always help.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah, is that sort of your ideal career then?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, definitely.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that there will be any barriers preventing you achieving that?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er, at the moment it's financial – you've got to have the capital to invest in the first place. Erm, but I'm quite lucky I've inherited enough so I can, you know, at least get one step on the ladder, so that's good.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Excellent. Would you like to work abroad or do you just want to go…?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Well - yeah, I wouldn't mind especially like somewhere like where it's hot. But that's the beauty of QS'ing as well. Because it's – you know – everything is a standard way of doing it you can work in other countries quite easily. Yeah, I would – you know, if there was a job going I definitely would.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that the career prospects are good in what you want to go into?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, I think so. You know there's always kind of jobs going – there's plenty in the papers and things. Cos there's so many companies as well and I think – I think the turnover is quite sort of rapid, so there are always jobs available.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, what about the prospects once you're into the industry then?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah I think it's good. I mean you do kind of – they encourage you to get your sort of chartership and they encourage you to go on courses. You get little ticks in your boxes for things, which is good. And CITB kind of help with all that as well. And you can do health and safety training and definitely, you can climb the ladder if you want to.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, are you happy with all the career choices you've made so far? Would you do anything differently if you had to do it all again?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, I probably wouldn't have chosen the company that I was sponsored by if I knew a bit more about it. 'Cos that's – you know I feel they didn't want me for who I was and I felt like, you know I was getting treated like that when I was working there. Erm, I think I would have chosen a smaller company. Yeah, definitely.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that the reason you were treated like that had anything to do with being female or do you just think it was just because you were a student or just the company?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think – there was that factor, you know, they only employed me because I was a girl and it – you know it looked good on their statistics, because I know, from my mum, they do get kind of extra bonuses for having female employees and they have an incentive. I definitely think it was – especially some of the older staff were like that.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What 5 words would you use to describe the construction industry?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Oh God. Erm, I suppose hard work is one (Yeah). Erm, I don't know, I suppose quite domineering and well it's fun as well and it's manual – hands on. That's 5 or 4?

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: When you say domineering, what do you mean by that?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Well, you have to be quite kind of forceful a bit, especially working with the men you've got to be quite quick witted and you know, show that you've got a bit of power – and it's quite a power trip when you're working, especially when you're working with the labourers - you know, they've come in and asked me for money. And you can say, well no, and you've got to be able to put your foot down but you've also got to be able to kind of take everything on the chin. You're always gonna get banter.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think there is conflict between being a good professional in the industry and being feminine?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, I felt, when I was working that they didn't – er it was weird because I felt like they only employed me because I was a girl and yet they didn't want me to act feminine. And so I kind of – you know – when I was going – you know getting – going out for drinks and stuff it was always – everyone kind of frowned upon iy and there was – you know – I was trying to be like one of the lads, you know, but there is this type of – they took it as you know, I was going on all these dates and things and you know - it was – they just didn't want me to act feminine. Kind of – you know – I got, when I was working there I got sort of advised how to dress – it was just like you know, well surely I can just sort of – if I want to wear a skirt, I can. You know there's definitely that aspect to it, yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, do you think that the engineering culture is masculine?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, definitely. I mean only due to the fact that sort of the actual work involves kind of – well hands on skills and things. So it's - I don't think it's because there's all these males in the industry it's just that's sort of the nature of the job.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think then that it will stay like that?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think so yeah, I know the year below, there's a few more girls on the course, which is good, but I think it's mainly gonna be sort of male dominated. I don't think it's gonna change,

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, that's everything I need – thank you very much.
